case_study_insert.main_stem: Greenbasket Organics (GBO) is a cooperative in the organic food retail sector, employing a workforce of 34. Founded in 2010 by Hannah Okafor, the members' cooperative runs two organic shops and a farm-box scheme in Riverton, operating a flat structure with democratic leadership. GBO plans to invest $640,000 in a third organic store with a home-delivery depot, financed by $400,000 member share capital and $240,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $198,000 a year, a variable cost of $2.20 a unit and a selling price of $5.50, and currently produces 78,000 units a year. GBO faces twin operational problems: seasonal staffing shortages run 28% above roster in the December peak and organic waste is running at 7.5% of stock.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2026: GBO recorded 7.5% organic waste worth $36,000 over the year, with 240 kg of unsold produce donated each week. The farm-box scheme delivered 6,800 boxes last quarter at a 98.2% on-time rate. A member survey of 350 respondents found 66% would join an expanded home-delivery scheme and 71% prefer local farms within 50 km. Average basket value is $28.40, breakage complaints fell from 24 to 11 per month, and the December peak requires 28 seasonal hires above roster.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Greenbasket Organics as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.2% from $12.75 to $13.41 per hour from April 2026, lifting seasonal and part-time wage bills. (3) Organic produce input costs (grain, dairy and fresh vegetables) have risen 11.2% year-on-year, organic food inflation is 7.4%, and consumer spending on organic products grew 6.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: GBO must finance part of the third store and home-delivery depot. Explain two advantages for GBO of using member share capital instead of the $240,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Member share capital carries no fixed interest or repayment, which matters when GBO's margins are tight — variable cost is $2.20 against a $5.50 selling price and organic waste already costs $36,000 a year. Avoiding loan repayments protects the cash needed for the $640,000 depot build and keeps the price of weekly farm boxes stable for price-sensitive member households.

Point 2: Raising money from members deepens the cooperative's democratic ethos and loyalty: the same members who invest are the 71% who prefer local farms within 50 km and the 66% who would join an expanded home-delivery scheme. Members who hold share capital are more likely to stay, shop and volunteer at the depot, strengthening GBO's local roots and making the launch less dependent on bank goodwill than the $240,000 bank loan alone would allow.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Greenbasket Organics, its cooperative structure and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: GBO is opening its third organic store with a home-delivery depot. Consider in-store tastings and farm open days, a local radio campaign, or social media food-blogger promotion. Which should GBO choose to promote the opening? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
In-store tastings and farm open days: Face-to-face events let Riverton members taste organic produce, meet the 50 km-radius farmers GBO buys from, and sign up for the expanded home-delivery scheme on the spot, directly converting the 71% local-farm preference and the 66% who would join delivery into sales. Events build the cooperative community spirit that differentiates GBO from supermarkets, and costs are mainly staff time and free samples; the limit is reach — only those who attend are persuaded, so coverage is slower and more manual than media.

Local radio campaign: Radio reaches car commuters and farm-box households across Riverton quickly and repeatedly, suits opening-week announcements and delivery-route launches, and a cooperative message about local sourcing can feel authentic on air. However, it is one-way, cannot demonstrate freshness or taste, and spend is wasted on non-organic households; measuring response beyond a generic mention is difficult.

Social media food-blogger promotion: Food and farm bloggers could show recipes, box contents and farm visits to health-conscious followers, with trackable links to sign up for delivery. It is inexpensive and measurable, but GBO's members skew toward families and older buyers who may not follow bloggers daily, and blogger endorsement can backfire if a post overlooks the 7.5% waste problem GBO is trying to fix.

Recommendation: GBO should choose in-store tastings and farm open days as the anchor promotion, supported by a light social media schedule. It converts local trust into subscriptions exactly where the 71% and 66% research points, costs little beyond produce already in store, and embodies cooperative values better than broadcast or influencer marketing. Radio is rejected as one-way and wasteful outside the organic segment, and blogger-first promotion is rejected as too narrow and fragile for a weekly grocery habit; a small influencer budget can amplify the open days rather than replace them.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to GBO.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of GBO with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of GBO with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and blogger-first promotion are rejected.

questions.question_text: GBO operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for GBO of democratic leadership when tackling its seasonal staffing shortage in the December peak.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives GBO's 34 staff and returning seasonal workers a genuine voice in building December rosters, so the people who know peak demand can flag gaps early rather than GBO discovering 28% under-staffing on the shop floor. Staff who help design rotas feel ownership, reducing absenteeism and no-shows in the exact weeks when basket sizes and footfall peak, protecting the 6,800 boxes a quarter delivered at 98.2% on-time.

Point 2: Participation satisfies social and esteem needs (Maslow), so seasonal hires are more likely to return next year, cutting the annual cost of re-recruiting and re-briefing. A flat structure also means Hannah Okafor hears directly from packers and drivers about damaged stock and breakage, feeding the quality loop that has already cut breakage complaints from 24 to 11 per month and the 7.5% waste figure.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GBO's seasonal peak and flat structure.

questions.question_text: GBO wants to motivate seasonal checkout and packing staff for the December peak. Consider a seasonal attendance bonus or a profit-sharing scheme for all staff. Which should GBO choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Seasonal attendance bonus: A fixed cash bonus for any seasonal worker achieving near-perfect attendance across the four-week peak directly attacks the roster crisis, since the December shortfall of 28 hires is partly driven by unpredictable absences. It is simple to administer for short contracts, immediately salient, easy to budget against the $198,000 fixed cost base, and needs no annual profit data. Its limits are that it rewards presence rather than care: a worker can attend daily yet mishandle produce, so it does not by itself reduce the $36,000 organic waste figure or lift service at the tills.

Profit-sharing scheme for all staff: Distributing a slice of annual cooperative surplus to permanent and seasonal staff alike aligns everyone with turnover growth, waste reduction below 7.5%, basket value above $28.40 and customer loyalty. It suits GBO's cooperative identity, rewards results not just showing up, and could lift retention so seasonal staff return each December. However, the reward is delayed until accounts close, weak for casuals on four-week contracts, may feel unfair if a bad weather week erases the surplus, and requires transparent surplus reporting GBO must prepare for every member.

Decision: GBO should choose a seasonal attendance bonus for the December cohort, keeping its existing profit-sharing for permanent members. The bonus targets the exact failure point — no-shows at peak when 28 extra hires are needed — is affordable, instant and easy to communicate to casuals, and can include a quality hurdle (breakage below a set rate) to blunt the careless-attendance weakness. A profit-sharing rollout now is rejected because it cannot motivate four-week seasonal staff whose contract may end before any payout, and because its administration cost outweighs gains in a peak crisis; GBO can extend it to high-performing seasonal staff next year once the depot opens.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivation schemes with limited application to GBO.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both schemes in the context of GBO.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both schemes in the context of GBO with a well-justified decision explaining why profit-sharing is rejected for the December cohort and an attendance bonus with a quality hurdle is preferred.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how GBO's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $198,000 ÷ ($5.50 − $2.20) = $198,000 ÷ $3.30 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 units a year.
Formula: Margin of safety = Actual output − Break-even output. Substitution: 78,000 − 60,000 = 18,000 units. Answer: margin of safety is 18,000 units a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways GBO's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. GBO's managers can compare the 18,000-unit margin of safety against the third store's early trading months to judge how quickly the depot must build volume before fixed costs of $198,000 are covered.
2. The $3.30 contribution per unit lets managers model box-scheme pricing, for example trimming a $0.20 promotion on the $28.40 basket shows the extra boxes needed to hold contribution, guiding loyalty offers to the 66% of members who would join delivery.
3. Pairing $198,000 fixed costs with unit cost ($198,000 ÷ 78,000 = $2.54, plus $2.20 = $4.74 per unit) shows whether waste at 7.5% worth $36,000 is pushing real unit cost above $4.74, and quantifies savings available from donation routes and better cold storage before the depot opens.
4. Managers can use labour productivity (78,000 units ÷ 34 staff ≈ 2,294 units per worker) to plan December rostering for the 28 seasonal hires, set bonus targets, and check whether the $240,000 bank loan drawdown stays ahead of wages without breaching the cooperative's democratic budget approvals.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) Margin of safety = 18,000 units | (iii) Four contextual uses: safety cushion of 18,000 units vs 78,000-unit output; $28.40 basket pricing vs $3.30 contribution; unit-cost benchmarking at $4.74 to attack 7.5% waste ($36,000); and productivity planning at 2,294 units per worker for the 28 seasonal December hires.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GBO's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has GBO's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.76 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.96 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.95 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.21 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $85,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $40,000 cash = $185,000; 2025 current assets = $105,000 + $75,000 + $95,000 = $275,000. 2024 cover = $185,000 ÷ $105,000 current liabilities = 1.76; 2025 cover = $275,000 ÷ $140,000 = 1.96. 2024 liquid cover = ($185,000 − $85,000) ÷ $105,000 = $100,000 ÷ $105,000 = 0.95; 2025 liquid cover = ($275,000 − $105,000) ÷ $140,000 = $170,000 ÷ $140,000 = 1.21.

Evaluation: GBO's liquidity has strengthened across the board. Cash rose sharply from $40,000 to $95,000, reflecting member share capital flowing in ahead of the depot, while inventories grew only modestly from $85,000 to $105,000 and trade receivables from $60,000 to $75,000 (local farm invoices and cooperative wholesale accounts). Current liabilities increased from $105,000 to $140,000 as GBO leaned more on supplier credit for fresh produce, yet the two cover measures still rose. Non-current assets climbed from $1,150,000 to $1,540,000, and capital employed from $1,235,000 to $1,600,000, consistent with near-complete preparation for the new store. One caution: 7.5% waste worth $36,000 means some 2025 inventory is at risk of never converting to sales, so healthy liquid cover depends on maintaining donation and markdown disciplines.

Conclusion: GBO's financial position has improved. Overall cover strengthened from 1.76 to 1.96 and the liquid cover from 0.95 to 1.21, meaning short-term debts are now comfortably covered without forced selling of perishable stock. GBO should still tighten terms with slower wholesale buyers and keep waste below 7.5% so liquidity converts into sustainable surplus for members and the new depot's launch.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of cash, inventory and liability movements and a justified conclusion on whether GBO's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GBO of introducing a home-delivery box scheme for its farm-box members.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The scheme directly answers the 66% of surveyed members who would join an expanded home-delivery service, locking in recurring weekly revenue and lifting the $28.40 average basket value as households add dairy, bakery and pantry items to each box. It deepens loyalty to local farms within 50 km (preferred by 71%), differentiates GBO from supermarkets, spreads fixed costs of $198,000 across more volume, and improves cash flow as members pay abonnement in advance of delivery.

Disadvantage: Home delivery adds vehicle, fuel, routing, packaging and driver costs that the $5.50 selling price and $2.20 variable cost must absorb, squeezing the $3.30 contribution per unit unless basket charges rise. Perishable produce travels unaccompanied to doorsteps, raising the risk that the existing 7.5% organic waste worth $36,000 grows through failed deliveries and spoilage, and December's 28-strong seasonal hire problem would strain the depot when volumes peak.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GBO's research data, waste problem and box-scheme economics.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 5.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in organic input costs will affect GBO. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (from 4.0% to 4.75%): GBO's $240,000 bank loan, if variable-rate, costs roughly $1,800 more a year, a negligible sum next to the $640,000 depot build and well within cooperative cash of $95,000. Higher rates make any future borrowings — for vehicles or cold storage — pricier, and could slow member house-price growth and spending, but organic spend still grew 6.1%, cushioning the effect. This is the smallest of the three threats and can be fixed by refinancing.

Minimum wage increase (5.2% rise to $13.41 per hour from April 2026): GBO's workforce is deliberately part-time and seasonal; the 34 permanent members plus 28 December seasonal hires work limited weekly hours. The annual wage bill is therefore modest (roughly $5,000–$10,000 extra a year, heavier in December), and can be partly offset by productivity rostering, multiskilling between till and packing, and the attendance bonus rather than blanket pay rises.

Input-cost inflation (11.2% rise in grain, dairy and fresh vegetables): produce is the dominant component of GBO's $2.20 variable cost per unit, around $1.85–$2.00 of it. A 11.2% rise adds roughly $0.22 per unit — about $17,000 a year on 78,000 units — and it compounds with the $36,000 waste already being thrown away, because every discarded kilogram now costs 11.2% more to buy. Organic food inflation is 7.4%, so full pass-through would push GBO's prices ahead of the market and risk member churn at the 66% delivery-scheme sign-up stage.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in organic input costs will have the greatest impact on GBO. It attacks GBO on two fronts — procurement cost and waste value — every single week, against a sector where consumer tolerance for price rises is capped by 7.4% inflation and where cooperative members are exceptionally price-aware. The wage rise is second (a few thousand dollars, peak-weighted), and the interest-rate move is trivial and fixable. GBO should respond by locking annual supply contracts with its 50 km farms, expanding donation and markdown processes to cut the 7.5% waste, and negotiating a small basket-fee increase rather than headline price rises.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to GBO.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GBO's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of GBO with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
